passage: In the playschool garden, five children lined up for the red slide. Ganga was third. She hopped from foot to foot. "Me now! Me now!" Pallavi Miss knelt beside her. "You're waiting so nicely. First Lina, then Babu, then you." Ganga held up her fingers and counted: one, two. Lina slid down. Babu slid down. Ganga's turn! At the bottom she ran straight to Miss. "I waited!" Miss gave her a high five. Then Ganga ran to the back of the line again, all by herself.

qa.q: Where was Ganga in the line for the red slide?
qa.a: Ganga was third.

qa.q: How was Ganga feeling while she hopped from foot to foot?
qa.a: She felt impatient and excited, wanting her turn right away.

qa.q: How did Pallavi Miss help Ganga keep waiting?
qa.a: She praised Ganga's waiting and said clearly who came first, so Ganga could count the turns on her fingers.

qa.q: What might Lina and Babu feel when Ganga waits instead of pushing?
qa.a: They likely feel it is fair and safe to take their turns without being pushed.

grounding: Shows a young child learning to wait for a turn at the slide, held steady by a teacher's praise and a clear order.

passage: The last bell had gone, rain was hammering the tin roof, and the queue for the one water cooler stretched past the notice board. Keerthana's van left in five minutes. She looked at the line: Class 3 kids, a boy with a cricket bat, her classmate Shreya near the front. Nobody would mind, surely. She slipped in beside Shreya and held her bottle under the tap. "Oi!" said a small girl behind. "We were all waiting!" Shreya didn't say anything, just looked at her, and that was worse. Keerthana's cheeks went hot. Half of her wanted to shout, "My van's leaving!" The other half pulled the bottle back. "Sorry. Go," she mumbled, and stepped aside, the half-filled bottle dripping.

qa.q: How long until Keerthana's van left?
qa.a: Her van left in five minutes.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when Shreya looked at her without a word?
qa.a: She felt guilty and embarrassed, cheeks hot, torn between defending herself and stepping back.

qa.q: What could Keerthana try next time she is in a hurry?
qa.a: She could ask the line politely whether she might go first because her van is leaving, instead of slipping in.

qa.q: How did the small girl behind see Keerthana's push?
qa.a: To her it was simply unfair, because they had all been waiting in the rain too.

grounding: Shows a child pushing ahead in a queue because she is in a hurry, then feeling a flash of guilt at how others react.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Went to the market with Papa on the city bus in Aizawl today. I noticed three things he did. Getting on, he said "Thank you, ma'am" to the conductor, Lalremsiami aunty, even though she only gave us tickets. At the vegetable stall a man pushed in front of us. Papa just waited. I was so annoyed! On the way back the bus lurched and Papa bumped an old lady's basket. He said sorry and picked up her oranges. She smiled and gave me one! Papa never told me to do any of this. But when we got off, I said thank you to the conductor too. She winked at me.
Ankita

qa.q: What did Papa say to the conductor when he got on?
qa.a: He said "Thank you, ma'am" to the conductor.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel when the man pushed in front?
qa.a: Ankita was annoyed, even though Papa stayed calm and simply waited.

qa.q: Why did Papa's way of teaching manners work?
qa.a: He never lectured; he thanked, waited and apologised himself, and Ankita copied the thank-you on the way out.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami aunty feel when passengers thank her?
qa.a: She probably feels noticed and pleased, which is why she winked at Ankita.

grounding: Ankita's diary shows a parent teaching public manners by example, thanking the conductor, waiting and apologising, and the child copying.

passage: The four of them had come to the city library to study for the chemistry test, but Dilnaz found an old photo of their teacher in a yearbook, and that was the end of studying. Afreen laughed so hard she snorted, which made Rukhsar laugh harder. Their table shook. Around them, heads lifted: an old man with a newspaper, a college student in earphones, a woman with a toddler asleep on her shoulder. Afreen didn't notice; the joke felt like the best thing all week. Then the librarian, Mr Pinto, walked over and crouched by their table. "Girls, I can see it's funny," he said quietly. "The baby over there just fell asleep. Maybe take the yearbook outside for five minutes?" Afreen looked across. The mother gave a small, tired smile. Afreen's face went warm. "Sorry, sir," she whispered, and they tiptoed out, still shaking with giggles.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz find in the yearbook?
qa.a: An old photo of their teacher.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling before and after Mr Pinto spoke?
qa.a: At first she felt giddy and delighted, then embarrassed once she saw the tired mother.

qa.q: Why did Mr Pinto's approach work?
qa.a: He spoke quietly, admitted the joke was funny, and gave a reason and a simple option, so the girls felt corrected, not shamed.

qa.q: What was it like for the mother with the sleeping toddler?
qa.a: She was probably tired and worried the noise would wake her child, and relieved when the girls stepped outside.

grounding: Shows teenagers laughing loudly in a library, caught up in their group's energy, and a calm word from the librarian correcting it.

subtype: Queue jumped by a well-connected person [Receiver]
passage:
Monday. Hafsa had been in the scholarship verification queue at the university office since eight, token 47, clutching her family's papers. At eleven, Madhav strolled past forty people, said "Uncle called ahead" to the clerk, and was done in five minutes. Nobody said a word. Hafsa's hands shook with anger. She said nothing either.
Wednesday. Back again, because one paper needed another stamp. A man in front of her muttered, "That's how it works. Why fight?" Hafsa nodded, and hated herself for nodding.
Friday. When a woman holding a note from "the minister's office" walked to the front, Hafsa heard her own voice: "Ma'am, we've all been here since eight. Please take a token." The clerk hesitated. Two others in the queue murmured agreement. The woman sighed and went to the back.

qa.q: What token number did Hafsa have on Monday?
qa.a: Token 47.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when Madhav was served in five minutes?
qa.a: She felt angry and helpless; her hands shook, but she stayed silent like everyone else.

qa.q: What changed by Friday, and why did it work?
qa.a: Hafsa spoke up politely, stating that everyone had waited since eight, and others backed her, so the woman had to take her place in the queue.

qa.q: How might the man who said "Why fight?" see the queue?
qa.a: He seems to have learned to accept unfairness as normal, protecting himself by not expecting better.

grounding: Shows a young woman watching well-connected people skip a queue, first accepting it in anger and helplessness, then objecting.

subtype: Giving up a seat or space [Actor]
passage:
Thursday, 9:40 p.m.
Crowded metro home, standing room only. I finally got a seat at the interchange and sank into it like a king. Two stops later a woman got on with one hand on her belly and a heavy office bag, clearly pregnant. The man next to me closed his eyes. The college boys opposite stared hard at their phones. I stood up and said, "Please sit." She said, "Thank you, I'm Ayesha, but I'll be fine for two stops." I said, "So will I." She sat. That was it. Nobody clapped. Honestly, my feet ached for the next forty minutes, and I was a bit grumpy about it. But I kept thinking of my sister last year, standing on a bus in her eighth month because nobody looked up. I'd rather be the one who looks up.
Pankaj

qa.q: How long did Pankaj's feet ache after standing up?
qa.a: For the next forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel after giving up the seat?
qa.a: Pankaj felt a bit grumpy about aching feet but settled about the choice, remembering the sister and not needing anyone to clap.

qa.q: What could other passengers learn from Pankaj?
qa.a: Looking up from the phone and offering a seat quietly takes a moment, and it matters without any applause.

qa.q: What might the ride have been like for Ayesha if no one had stood?
qa.a: She would have stood with a heavy bag while pregnant, probably tired and uncomfortable, like Pankaj's sister last year.

grounding: Pankaj's diary shows a young adult giving up a metro seat to a pregnant woman out of awareness, with no need for praise.

passage: I'm Dolma. Last week, at the shared-taxi stand in Gangtok, I watched a young man in a bright jacket finish his cold drink and toss the bottle over the railing into the jhora. Four of us were waiting. The driver looked away. My friend Lalremsiami raised her eyebrows at me. My first thought was a scolding: "Is this your house, to throw things anywhere?" Then I noticed his two friends, loud and restless, and the empty road. A fight over a bottle wasn't worth it. So I said, lightly, "Arre, the stream's already so full, na? There's a bin by the tea stall." He looked embarrassed, laughed and said, "Sorry, didi." He didn't climb down for the bottle. But when his friend finished a drink, he pointed at the bin.

qa.q: Where did the young man toss his bottle?
qa.a: Over the railing into the jhora.

qa.q: What was going on in Dolma's mind before speaking?
qa.a: Dolma felt irritated and wanted to scold, but was cautious about the loud friends and the empty road, and worried a fight could follow.

qa.q: Why did Dolma's light comment work better than a scolding might have?
qa.a: It pointed to the bin without insulting him, so he could laugh, apologise and change without losing face in front of his friends.

qa.q: How might the young man have felt when Dolma spoke?
qa.a: He likely felt a bit embarrassed but not attacked, which is why he said sorry and later pointed his friend to the bin.

grounding: Dolma watches someone litter, weighs safety and tone, and chooses a light, polite comment over a scolding.

passage:
"Excuse me," Elizabeth said, smiling, as Kashish stepped in front of her at the bakery counter. "The queue begins back there, by the door."
Kashish turned, surprised. "Oh! Does it? I thought this was the pickup counter."
"Easy to miss. The sign's tiny."
"Sorry, sorry." Kashish went to the back. The old man behind Elizabeth chuckled. "Nicely done."
Ten minutes later a man in a gym vest walked straight to the till. "Sorry, the queue begins by the door," Elizabeth said, same tone.
"Mind your own business," he snapped.
The cashier glanced at her. Elizabeth shrugged. "Fine. Go ahead."
"You're letting him?" whispered the old man.
"It's two croissants," Elizabeth said. "Not worth a fight."
From the back of the line, Kashish laughed. "You were right the first time, though."

qa.q: Where does the queue begin, according to Elizabeth?
qa.a: The queue begins back there, by the door.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth let the man in the gym vest go ahead?
qa.a: She stayed calm but was cautious; once he turned hostile, she felt a fight over two croissants was not worth it.

qa.q: What made Elizabeth's first request work with Kashish?
qa.a: She smiled, said where the queue begins without accusing, and offered an easy reason for the mistake.

qa.q: How might Kashish have felt on being told about the line?
qa.a: Kashish was surprised and a little embarrassed but not humiliated, since the tone was friendly, so moving to the back felt easy.

grounding: Shows a person calmly and warmly enforcing a queue, which works, and letting it go when someone turns hostile.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, Friday.
Pema came to school today in a yellow team shirt three sizes too big, the number on the back taped where it had torn. It was the morning after the local club won the state football final. Before assembly Pema had a circle of six children around him, acting out the last goal with a lunch box as the ball. Chandrika, who supports the same club, kept shouting "We won! We!" as though she had played. Even Tsering, who usually hangs back, joined the chant. In maths Pema drew the club badge in the margin and wrote OUR TEAM. I let the shirt stay today and asked Pema to write three sentences about the match for English. He wrote seven.

qa.q: What colour was Pema's team shirt?
qa.a: A yellow team shirt, three sizes too big.

qa.q: How can you tell Pema felt proud to be one of the club's fans?
qa.a: He wore the huge shirt, acted out the goal for friends and wrote OUR TEAM, which shows pride and a strong sense of belonging.

qa.q: How did the teacher make good use of Pema's excitement?
qa.a: The teacher let the shirt stay and turned the excitement into writing about the match, so Pema wrote seven sentences instead of three.

qa.q: What might the win have felt like for Tsering, who usually hangs back?
qa.a: Joining the chant probably felt like an easy way in, being part of "we" without having to say much.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a child whose love for a football club gives him instant belonging and a shared story with other fans.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Tuesday.
Simran, Class 10, came to see me after a fight in the canteen. Her bag is covered in pins from a boy band from Seoul; her pencil case, even the margins of her notebooks, carry their lyrics. At lunch her friend Uma called the band's new song "lazy" in front of four others. Simran told me, "It felt like she was saying I'm lazy." She shouted, Uma walked off, and the rest of the table took sides. Simran was close to tears describing the fan group online: "They get me. My class doesn't." I didn't criticise the band. I asked what the music gave her; she talked about a hard year and one song that got her through it. Then we talked about how Uma can dislike a song and still like her. She plans to find Uma after practice. I'll check in with her on Friday.

qa.q: What did Uma call the band's new song?
qa.a: Uma called it "lazy".

qa.q: Why did Uma's remark hurt Simran so much?
qa.a: The band is part of who Simran is, so she felt personally attacked and defensive, as if Uma had called her lazy.

qa.q: What might help Simran when she talks with Uma after practice?
qa.a: Separating the song from herself: explaining that the music got her through a hard year, and that Uma can dislike it and still be her friend.

qa.q: How might Uma see the canteen fight?
qa.a: Uma may have meant it as an ordinary opinion about a song and felt hurt and confused by the shouting.

grounding: The counsellor's note shows a teenager whose fandom is part of her identity, feeling understood by fans and defensive when her band is criticised.
